summary: Peru grants visa-free entry to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas — 90 days, extendable once by 90 days within a year, for most of them, and 90 days in any 180 for EU and Schengen-area passports — records arrivals by air digitally, and lets Chinese and Indian citizens who hold a valid US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa enter without a Peruvian visa.

fee.notes: Peru's Consular Fee Schedule sets a fixed S/C 30 for a tourist visa (tariff 67a; one consular sol equals USD 1). The payment is not refunded if the visa is refused. The Foreign Ministry's tourist-visa page (gob.pe/36240) says the 183-day stay comes "sin posibilidad de prórroga" (no extension), though a later line mentions applying to Migraciones for one.

source.name: Ministerio de Relaciones Exteriores del Perú — Tabla de Tarifas de Derechos Consulares
source.instrument: Tarifa de Derechos Consulares, Sección VII, tarifa 67 a)

passportValidity.text: Migraciones says a passport valid for at least six months is mandatory, and that without it you cannot enter Peru.

source.name: Superintendencia Nacional de Migraciones — Información fundamental para turistas en Perú

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: Not required for entry, but Peru's health ministry says travellers heading to jungle areas should be vaccinated at least 10 days before the trip. The endemic areas are the forested jungle of Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín, Ucayali and Amazonas (Iquitos, Puerto Maldonado, Tarapoto) and the jungle zones of Junín, Ayacucho, Cusco, Huánuco, Pasco and Puno — Machu Picchu and the Inca Trail are excluded.

source.name: Ministerio de Salud del Perú (MINSA) — Vacúnate contra la fiebre amarilla

travelInsurance.text: No official source we could read states a travel insurance requirement for entry to Peru; Migraciones' guidance for tourists does not mention it.

source.name: Superintendencia Nacional de Migraciones — Información fundamental para turistas en Perú

onwardTicket.text: No official source we could read states an onward or return ticket requirement for entry to Peru. Canada's travel advice says customs officials may ask to see a return or onward ticket.

source.name: Government of Canada — Peru travel advice: entry and exit requirements

proofOfFunds.text: No official source we could read states a proof-of-funds requirement or amount for Peru. Canada's travel advice says officials may ask for proof that you have a place to stay and sufficient funds for the duration of your stay.

source.name: Government of Canada — Peru travel advice: entry and exit requirements

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments over USD 10,000 (or equivalent) must be declared on arrival and departure; carrying more than USD 30,000 in cash is prohibited.

source.name: SUNAT — Ingresar y salir con dinero del país

notes: Canada's travel advice says Peru's international airports do not stamp passports and keep digital entry and exit records instead; Migraciones says you can check your authorized stay by downloading your virtual Andean Migration Card (TAM).
The UK government says it is illegal to remove any archaeological artefacts from Peru without authorisation.
The UK government advises against taking coca leaves or coca tea out of Peru, as importing them into the UK is illegal.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice says the US dollar is widely accepted, credit cards are not commonly accepted outside major cities, many establishments ask to see a passport when you pay by card, and ATMs are not easily found in small towns and often limit withdrawals.

safety.text: The UK Foreign Office says street crime, including muggings and thefts, is a significant problem in Lima, Cusco, Arequipa and other major cities; that tourists, especially those travelling alone, are at risk of 'express kidnapping', often by criminals posing as taxi drivers; and that the border areas with Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil and the VRAEM carry a higher risk because of organised crime linked to drug production. It advises licensed telephone or app-based taxis rather than hailing one on the street.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Peru travel advice: safety and security

bestTimeToVisit.text: Canada's travel advice says the rainy season in the Peruvian Andes runs from November to May, when flooding and landslides can close tourist areas, and that forest fires are common in the dry season from June to October.

idp.text: Peru is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Peru is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Peru yet.

tips.text: The UK government says altitude sickness is a serious risk in parts of Peru, including Cusco, Puno, the Colca Canyon and Kuelap. Canada's travel advice says the risk starts at 2,500 metres and is higher if you ascend quickly or exercise or drink alcohol before you get used to the altitude.

The UK government warns of robberies by criminals posing as taxi drivers, especially at Lima's Jorge Chávez airport and bus terminals, and advises licensed telephone or app-based taxis, hotel-booked taxis, or the official taxi desks outside the airport baggage hall.
Australia's Smartraveller advises drinking boiled or bottled water in Peru.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Peru visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days, extendable once for another 90 days within 365 days of first entry. Canada's travel advice says entry by air is recorded digitally rather than stamped in the passport.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Peru as a tourist?
faq.answer: It depends on your passport. Most visa-exempt visitors get 90 days, extendable once for another 90 days within 365 days of first entry; EU and Schengen-area passports (and those of Georgia, Russia, Turkey and Ukraine) get 90 days in any 180-day period; Mexico, El Salvador and Qatar get 183 days, Barbados, Costa Rica, Honduras and Panama 90 days, and the Dominican Republic 60 days, none of them extendable.

faq.question: Do Chinese or Indian citizens need a visa for Peru?
faq.answer: Normally yes — a consular tourist visa. However, Chinese and Indian citizens holding a US, UK, Canadian, Australian or Schengen visa valid for at least six months (or permanent residence in those places) can enter Peru without a Peruvian visa for tourism or business, for up to 180 days within 365 days of first entry, not extendable.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccine for Machu Picchu or the Amazon?
faq.answer: Not for Machu Picchu or the Inca Trail, which Peru's health ministry excludes. It recommends vaccination at least 10 days before travel to jungle areas: the forested jungle of Loreto, Madre de Dios, San Martín, Ucayali and Amazonas (Iquitos, Puerto Maldonado, Tarapoto) and the jungle zones of Junín, Ayacucho, Cusco region, Huánuco, Pasco and Puno.

faq.question: Do I need to fill in an entry form (TAM) for Peru?
faq.answer: No official source we could read describes an entry form to fill in. Canada's travel advice says Peru's international airports keep digital entry and exit records instead of stamping passports, and Migraciones says you can check your authorized stay by downloading your virtual Andean Migration Card (TAM).
